one_liner: DynamoRIO-based memory error checker for unmodified binaries; about 2x faster than Valgrind Memcheck on SPEC CPU2006 per its CGO 2011 paper.
what_it_does: Dr. Memory runs an unmodified application binary under the DynamoRIO dynamic binary instrumentation framework and reports uninitialized reads, unaddressable accesses (heap overflow/underflow, use-after-free), double frees, mismatched free/delete, memory leaks and, on Windows, handle leaks, GDI API misuse and unreserved TLS slot access. Like Memcheck it needs no recompilation (`drmemory -- ./app`), but its option set and report format are its own. The package also ships drstrace (an strace for Windows), drltrace and drfuzz.
how_it_is_fast: It keeps shadow memory for every application byte and inlines a fast path for the common shadow check into DynamoRIO's code cache, dropping to a slow path only for uncommon cases (the paper per search snippets describes these fastpath/slowpath instrumentation optimizations as the source of the 2x average gain over Memcheck). It replaces malloc with its own allocator instead of wrapping it (-replace_malloc, on by default). Cheaper modes trade coverage for speed: -light and -no_check_uninitialized skip definedness tracking, -pattern uses sentinel values around heap blocks instead of shadow memory, -leaks_only checks leaks only, and -persist_code caches instrumented code across runs.
when_to_use: Memory-error checking of Windows binaries, especially closed-source or third-party ones you cannot rebuild with AddressSanitizer: Valgrind does not run on Windows.
Linux x86/x86-64 CI jobs where Valgrind Memcheck is too slow and recompiling with ASan is not possible.
Hunting uninitialized reads in binaries, which ASan does not detect (MSan needs a full instrumented rebuild).
Fast smoke runs with -light or -leaks_only when only unaddressable accesses or leaks matter.
when_not_to_use: When you can recompile: the sibling AddressSanitizer pages list about 2x slowdown for ASan vs about 10x for Dr. Memory and 20x for Memcheck.
When you need current, documented performance numbers: the only head-to-head data is the 2011 paper against the Valgrind of that time, and its chart is on a blocked host.

AArch64/ARM or macOS 64-bit: optionsx.h notes only pattern mode is supported on ARM (no uninitialized-read checks); 64-bit coverage gaps are open issues (e.g. #1632 byte-to-byte shadowing for 64-bit).
Programs heavy in SIMD code: issues #1525 and #1562 note xmm operations still go through the slow path, and issue #1188 reports a 29x slowdown on wrf from 185M uninitialized-value events.
If you need a stable release cadence: releases are automated cronbuild packages (latest cronbuild-2.6.20434, December 2024) and the tracker has about 1,000 open issues.

integration.dependencies: DynamoRIO (a dynamorio directory in the repo tree; prebuilt packages include everything)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented in the README (CMake build; binary packages recommended)
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux, Mac, Android on IA-32, AMD64 and ARM (README); ARM limited to pattern mode
integration.thread_safety: Supports multi-threaded applications (it is a whole-process tool); per-option thread behaviour not documented in the README
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same run-the-binary workflow as valgrind --tool=memcheck, but different command line, suppression format and reports

gotchas: -pattern and -unaddr_only disable uninitialized-read checks; -no_check_uninitialized also lowers leak-identification accuracy (optionsx.h).
With -no_check_uninitialized, unaligned accesses and stack-relative references are not checked unless -check_alignment / -check_stack_access are set, so some overflows can be missed.
Symbol processing can dominate startup on large Windows apps (issue #2175: msvcr120d.dll 40 s even with symcache; #1447 online symbolization bottleneck).
License is LGPL-2.1-only for the core; drfuzz and drltrace are BSD.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Dr. Memory over AddressSanitizer when you cannot rebuild the target or need uninitialized-read checks on Windows, and over RetroWrite (binary-rewriting ASan, benchmarked on Linux SPEC CPU2006) when the binary is on Windows; if recompiling is possible, ASan is several times faster.
verified_claims_summary: The README states Dr. Memory beats Valgrind on SPEC CPU2006 on Linux and points to a bar chart from the peer-reviewed CGO 2011 paper (Bruening and Zhao); search snippets of that paper give a 2x average and up to 4x per-benchmark speedup over Memcheck, with Memcheck failing on 434.zeusmp and 447.dealII. CPU, compiler flags and the Valgrind version were not visible because the paper and chart hosts are blocked; independent support comes from the sanitizers comparison table (Dr. Memory about 10x vs Memcheck about 20x slowdown).
status_note: Maintained at a low pace (last commit 2025-12-12, automated cronbuild releases, 57 open Performance-labelled issues), LGPL-2.1 so usable as an external tool without licensing concerns.
sources_read: WebSearch: "Practical Memory Checking with Dr. Memory" CGO 2011 (snippets)
